newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Problems mount for Irish pension system.
newsitem.headline: Problems mount for Irish pension system.

text.p: Ireland's public pensions scheme is about to confront the same problems of dealing with an ageing population that other European countries have had to face in recent years.
The country's 3.65 million population will present the next generation with a punishing pensions bill.
"In 1990 the population over 65 was 33,950. By the year 2030 it will be 646,000," Irish Association of Pension Funds (IAPF) chairman, Brian Aylward says.
Aylward said the level of pensions cover currently taken out is very inadequate and the state has not, as yet, made any special provisions for the growing number of retired people.
"In the private sector there is only 38 percent (pension) cover. This compares to 83 percent in Holland and over 52 percent in the UK," Aylward said.

He said not only will the next century see the number of pensioners jump it will also see an increase in the numbers over 80 years of age which he said will also mean larger medical bills for that section of the population.

The combination of falling birthrates and greater longevity among the population will combine to dramatically increase those in need of pensions. However the workforce to support the the system will have seriously contracted.

"Basically each generation is paying, not for themselves, but for the pensioners in their time. At the moment there are six workers paying PRSI (pay-related-social-insurance) for every one pensioner," said National Pensions Board chief executive Ann Maher said.
Maher said by the year 2035 the number of workers relative to pensioners is going to drop to about three to one.
"When this drops down to three people per pensioner either the pensioner receives less or the worker pays more," Maher said.

Maher said Ireland is in a better position than other European states as the problems of coping with an ageing population are taking longer to arrive than in other countries so "... we will have the experience of other countries to learn from".
"We are starting to look at pension reform now and we are doing so not as a result of a crisis which will allow us time to address and change things in a measured way."
Ireland's pensions problems became a live issue after the publication of a study by the state-funded Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) and the semi-state Pensions Board last October.

While statistics showed 52 per cent of the workforce was covered by pension schemes, a more in depth look showed that 83 percent of that cover was due to (non-contributory) public sector pensions and it did not include self-employed persons or farmers.
In fact only 38 per cent of those in the private sector were covered by pension schemes.

"The other cause of concern is that the state pension, which is a standard flat rate pension, is normally increased in line with the price index but it is falling away in the sense that it is not related to earnings," Maher said.
"As a percentage of your actual industrial earnings it is actually declining that will be a problem down the line for people."
Employment trends show an increasing shift towards self-employed and part-time or temporary employment.
Cover for self-employed persons currently runs at about 27 per cent while part-time workers cover is as low as 11 per cent.
"The ERSI study certainly revealed very disappointing levels of pension cover," Paul O'Faherty, director of pension consultants Mercer Ltd said.
"It has prompted a fair level of debate on the future of pensions cover and a consultative document is underway to look at the way forward and the possible solutions."
